manufacturer.trigem.description: South Korean computer manufacturer also known as Sambo Computer and TG Sambo, active under its own brands and as an international OEM.
manufacturer.trigem.history:
TriGem was founded on 2 July 1980 in Seoul's Cheonggyecheon district as Sambo Engineering: seven engineers led by Lee Yong-tae, with ten million won of capital. "Sambo" means "three jewels", hence the English name TriGem, which the company used until 2002.

Its first computer was the SE-8001 of September 1981, with 48 KB of memory, which the company itself presents as the first PC made in South Korea and which was used mainly for business accounting. In June 1982 it sold 1,200 TriGem 20 computers to Canada, the country's first computer export according to its own chronology, and in 1983 it launched the TriGem 20XT, an 8-bit machine of which it sold about 6,000 units in a year. By the mid-1980s the company was also working with Seiko Epson on printers and developing its own software, such as the Korean word processor Bosuk-geul.

With the arrival of IBM PC compatibles, TriGem combined two businesses. It sold computers under its own brand in Korea and, at the same time, built motherboards and complete machines for other companies, which sold them under their own names. In the early 1990s it joined the American company CMS Enhancements to build CMS-branded PCs; the 1992 price war sank the project and very few were sold. Boards from that period survive, such as the SX386M, an 80386SX found inside the Emerson Elite SX386/16 and the CMS ESP SX386M.

Building for others reached its most visible point in 1998, when TriGem and Korea Data Systems created eMachines in the United States. Its first eTower models cost $399 and $499 without a monitor, and by March 1999 the brand was fourth in US sales. Gateway bought eMachines in 2004.

In 2002 the company was renamed TG Sambo. Falling exports, under competition from Chinese and Taiwanese manufacturers, led it to apply for court receivership in May 2005. Celrun bought it in 2007 and the receivership ended in 2008; in 2012 the computer business moved to a new company that keeps the Sambo Computer name. TG&Co., established in 2011, keeps 1980 as the starting point of its own chronology.
